_note: Spoken guide scripts, one per destination slug. Recorded to media/audio/guide-<slug>.mp3 by voice_guides.py in the site voice, Jason. Every guide must run at least three minutes of speech, roughly 500 words or more, and voice_guides.py refuses to record one shorter, so a short script here is a to-do, not a guide. Write for the ear: short sentences, concrete detail, one thing worth remembering and one thing to do, and no long dashes.
pike-place-market:
Pike Place Market. It has been open since 1907, which makes it the oldest continuously operating farmers market in the country, and it very nearly was not any of this. By the nineteen sixties the city had a plan to knock the whole thing down and put up parking and office towers, and it took a public vote, a ballot measure the people of Seattle passed themselves, to save it. So everything you are about to walk through is here because a city was asked, and said keep it. Come hungry, wear shoes you can stand in for a while, and give it at least twice the time you were planning to.

Start at the front, under the big clock and the red neon sign, because that is where the show is. The fish market at the corner is the one you have seen. The men behind the counter throw the fish. A customer orders a salmon, someone shouts, and a whole king salmon flies over the ice to be caught and wrapped. It looks like a stunt for tourists, and it actually started as a shortcut, a way to move fish from the front ice to the back counter without walking it around. Stand and watch a few go by. It is free, and it is genuinely good.

Then go deeper, because the front is the least of it. The market is nine acres, and it runs down the hillside for several floors below the main street, a warren of stairways and corridors most visitors never find. There are farm stalls where the person selling you the peaches is the person who grew them, a rule the market takes seriously. There are flower stalls where an armful of dahlias costs less than a sandwich, and you should buy some even if you have nowhere to put them. There are tiny counters selling noodles and piroshki and chowder, comic shops, a magic store, and record bins, all folded into the same building.

A few things to find. The first Starbucks is across the street at 1912 Pike Place, still small, still busy, with the original sign in the window, though the honest truth is it moved a block from its very first location, so it is the oldest one still open rather than the exact first. Down a flight of stairs off Post Alley is the gum wall, which is exactly what it sounds like, and is either delightful or revolting depending on your temperament. And near the fish counter, look down for Rachel, a bronze piggy bank the size of a real pig, who has been swallowing tourists' coins for decades, all of it going back into the market's own services for the people who live and work here.

The rhythm of the place is worth knowing. Go early if you want the flowers and the produce at their best and the aisles still walkable. Go late morning if you want the full crowd and the full noise. Either way, do not eat before you come. The right way to do this market is to graze your way through it, a bite here and a cup of chowder there, and to buy something you did not plan to buy from someone who made it. Keep an hour more than you think you need. Everyone always does.
the-met-museum: The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Five thousand years of human making under one roof on Fifth Avenue. Nobody sees it all; pick two wings and walk them slowly. The Temple of Dendur, an actual Egyptian temple, sits in a hall of glass, and the rooftop in summer has a skyline view most visitors never find. Give it three hours and it will still be the fastest three hours of your trip.
staten-island-ferry: The Staten Island Ferry. Completely free, running all day and all night, and quietly one of the best boat rides in America. Twenty five minutes across the harbor, past the Statue of Liberty, with the whole downtown skyline stacked up behind you. Ride out, walk off, and take the next boat straight back. Stand on the right side going out; that is where the Statue is.
space-needle:
The Space Needle. It was built for the 1962 World's Fair, in a year when the country wanted to look like the future, and more than sixty years later it is still the shape the whole Seattle skyline is drawn around. The idea started as a sketch in a coffee shop, a drawing of a balloon tethered to the ground, and the men behind the fair had less than a year to turn it into steel. They dug a hole thirty feet deep and poured a foundation that weighs almost exactly as much as the tower standing on it, which is the reason it does not sway the way your stomach expects a tower to sway. It has ridden out earthquakes and hundred mile an hour wind, and it was built to. You are safe up here. Let that go, and look.

Take the elevator. It climbs at about ten miles an hour, roughly the speed of a raindrop falling, and in forty three seconds the doors open five hundred and twenty feet up. The observation level at the top is open to the air on every side, so the wind and the sound of the city come up to meet you, and there is nothing between you and the view but a rail and some angled glass. Walk the whole way around before you settle anywhere. People plant themselves at the first thing they see and miss half of it.

Here is what you are looking at. To the south, on a day when the clouds cooperate, Mount Rainier stands on the horizon like it was pasted there, more than fourteen thousand feet of it, close enough to feel and far enough that it never quite looks real. To the west is Elliott Bay and the working waterfront, the ferries crossing to the islands, and behind them the jagged line of the Olympic Mountains across the Sound. North is Lake Union with the little seaplanes lifting off the water, and east are the Cascades and the neighborhoods climbing the hills. The whole geography of the city explains itself from up here in about two minutes, which is something no map ever manages.

Then go down one level, because most people forget it is there. The floor below the top slowly rotates, a full turn in about three quarters of an hour, and the floor itself is glass, a ring of it called the Loupe, the first revolving glass floor ever built. You stand on it and the city moves under your feet, five hundred feet of open air straight down through the soles of your shoes. Some people cannot do it. Most people cannot stop once they start. There are glass benches too, tilted out over the edge, if you want to lean back against nothing at all.

One piece of advice worth more than the ticket. The sunset slots are the first to sell out, and they sell out for a reason. Book the hour before the light goes gold, ride up while it is still day, and stay through the moment the city switches its lights on beneath you. You will feel the whole deck go quiet when it happens. Bring a layer. It is colder and windier up here than it was on the ground, and you are going to want to stay longer than you think.
bainbridge-island-ferry: The Bainbridge Island Ferry. Thirty five minutes across Puget Sound on a working state ferry, with the Seattle skyline shrinking behind you and the Olympic mountains ahead. Walk on, no reservation, and the fare is only collected leaving Seattle, so the ride home is free. On the island, Winslow's main street is ten minutes on foot from the dock: bookshops, bakeries, and a harbor full of sailboats.
lincoln-memorial:
The Lincoln Memorial. It is open every hour of every day, it costs nothing, and it is at its best at the two ends of the day, early in the morning before the buses, or late at night when it is lit and nearly empty and the marble seems to hold its own light. However you come, do two things. Turn around, and read the walls.

First the building itself. It was finished in 1922, designed by Henry Bacon to look like a Greek temple, because the man inside it saved the republic that took its ideas from Greece. Count the columns. There are thirty six on the outside, one for every state in the Union at the moment Lincoln died. Higher up, carved above them, are the names of the states that existed when the memorial was built, and the last two, Alaska and Hawaii, are added on a plaque by the steps. Nothing here is decoration. Every number is counting something.

Then go up the steps and inside, and there he is. The statue is nineteen feet of white Georgia marble, Lincoln seated, and it was carved by Daniel Chester French, who thought hard about the hands. Look at them. One is closed in a fist, one is open and at rest, and people have read a hundred meanings into that, strength and mercy, war and peace, though the sculptor mostly wanted them to look like a real man's hands. The face is tired. That was on purpose too. This is not a triumphant Lincoln. It is a Lincoln who has carried something.

Now read the walls, because this is the part most people skip, and it is the whole point. On the south wall, to your right as you face him, the Gettysburg Address is carved in full, and it is shorter than any speech you have ever had to sit through, two minutes to read, and it reorganizes the entire meaning of the country in under three hundred words. On the north wall is the Second Inaugural, given a month before he was killed, with malice toward none, and it is the more remarkable of the two, a wartime president refusing to gloat. Read them slowly. They were written to be read slowly.

Then walk back out to the top of the steps and turn around, and understand where you are standing. Down on the landing, about eighteen steps below the entrance, there is an engraving cut into the stone that marks the exact spot where Martin Luther King stood. On an August day in 1963 he stood there and spoke to a quarter of a million people who filled the ground from your feet to the Washington Monument, and told them about a dream. From up here the whole line of it opens in front of you, the long Reflecting Pool, the Monument at the far end, and the Capitol a straight mile beyond. That sightline is not an accident. The city was built to make you feel the weight of it, and standing here, at either end of a quiet day, it works. Give it time. There is nowhere on the Mall that rewards standing still like this one does.
empire-state-building: The Empire State Building. Eighty six floors up, and it opened in 1931, built in just over a year while the country was falling apart. The open air deck is the one you came for; the higher 102nd floor is glassed in and quieter. Go early, before ten, or late, after nine, and skip the middle of the day entirely. And look down: the whole grid of Manhattan lays itself out beneath you like a drawing.
central-park: Central Park. Eight hundred and forty three acres, and every inch of it is man made, designed in 1858 and built out of swamp and rock. Enter at Bethesda Terrace for the fountain and the arcade, walk north into the Ramble to get pleasantly lost, and finish at Belvedere Castle for the view. Give it two hours. Give it a whole afternoon if the weather is kind.
brooklyn-bridge: The Brooklyn Bridge. Walk it from the Brooklyn side toward Manhattan; that is the direction where the skyline opens in front of you instead of behind. Finished in 1883, it was the longest suspension bridge in the world, built with cables spun in place over the East River. The walk is about a mile, twenty five minutes at a stroll, and the pedestrian deck sits above the traffic. Early morning has the light and none of the crowd.
9-11-memorial-and-museum: The 9/11 Memorial. Two square voids, set exactly in the footprints of the towers, with water falling into them and disappearing into a second void below. Every name is cut into the bronze around the edges. The memorial outside is free and open; the museum below is a separate ticket and takes at least two hours. Take your time on the parapets. Some of the names have a white rose in them: that is somebody's birthday, placed there that morning.
grand-central-terminal: Grand Central Terminal. Look up first: the ceiling is a sky map with twenty five hundred stars, and it is painted backwards, as if you were looking down at the heavens from outside. Nobody has ever fully settled why. Then find the Whispering Gallery outside the Oyster Bar, stand facing a corner of the arch, and have someone stand at the opposite corner. Speak softly. They will hear you across the room.
the-high-line: The High Line. An abandoned elevated freight line that was going to be demolished, saved by two neighbors who went to a community meeting and found they were the only people in the room who wanted to keep it. Now it is a mile and a half of garden running thirty feet above the West Side. Walk it north from Gansevoort Street, and notice the planting: much of it is descended from the weeds that grew on the tracks while the line sat empty for twenty five years.
times-square: Times Square. It was Longacre Square until the New York Times moved in and put its name on the station in 1904. Everything you are looking at is legally required: the zoning here mandates a minimum amount of illuminated signage, so the lights are not excess, they are code. Come after dark, which is when it does what it does. Keep your wallet in a front pocket, and do not pay anyone in a costume.
chihuly-garden-and-glass: Chihuly Garden and Glass. Right at the foot of the Space Needle, and the best hour in Seattle Center. Eight galleries of blown glass, then a glass house with a hundred foot sculpture hanging overhead, then a garden where the glass grows among the real plants and you stop being sure which is which. Under an hour if you rush, and you should not rush.
gas-works-park: Gas Works Park. An abandoned gasification plant the city refused to tear down, so it kept the rusting towers and built a park around them. Climb the kite hill for the best skyline view in Seattle, with Lake Union and the seaplanes coming in below you. Sunset here is the local answer to the Space Needle, and it is free.
kerry-park-viewpoint: Kerry Park. It is barely a park, just a terrace on the side of Queen Anne hill, and it is the postcard: the Space Needle, downtown, Elliott Bay, and on a clear day Mount Rainier floating behind all of it. Five minutes to see, an hour if you wait for the light. Come at dusk when the city turns its lights on.
museum-of-pop-culture: The Museum of Pop Culture. The building is a Frank Gehry, and the story is that he cut up electric guitars and used the pieces as the model. Inside: Hendrix, Nirvana, science fiction, horror, and a tower built from six hundred instruments. Two hours, and it is the one museum in town where you are supposed to make noise.
seattle-aquarium: The Seattle Aquarium. Built right out over Elliott Bay on Pier 59, so the water under your feet is the same water in the tanks. The window on Puget Sound is the one to sit at: everything in it lives just outside. Ninety minutes, and check the feeding times when you walk in, because those are the fifteen minutes worth planning around.
starbucks-reserve-roastery: The Starbucks Reserve Roastery. Not the little store at Pike Place, this is the other one, fifteen thousand square feet of working roastery on Capitol Hill, with copper casks, coffee moving overhead through tubes, and a bar where they make things you cannot order anywhere else. Free to walk in, and worth it even if you do not drink coffee.
washington-monument: The Washington Monument. Five hundred and fifty five feet of marble, and if you look closely about a third of the way up, the stone changes color. Construction stopped for twenty three years when the money ran out and the Civil War came, and when they started again the original quarry was gone. The line in the stone is the war. Tickets to go up are a dollar and they go fast; the grounds are free and open all night.
jefferson-memorial: The Jefferson Memorial. Across the Tidal Basin, which is why most visitors look at it from a distance and never walk over. Do walk over. It is a domed rotunda open on every side, his words cut into the walls around the statue, and it is quieter than anything on the Mall. In late March and early April the cherry trees around the basin are the reason the whole city fills up.
lincoln-memorial-steps: The Lincoln Memorial steps. Find the engraving on the landing, about eighteen steps up: it marks the exact spot where Martin Luther King stood in August 1963. From there, the Reflecting Pool, the Washington Monument and the Capitol line up in a single straight mile, and that is the view a quarter of a million people were looking back from that day.
air-and-space-museum: The Air and Space Museum. The Wright Flyer, the Spirit of St. Louis, and the Apollo 11 command module are all in the same building, and it is free. Start upstairs and work down, because the crowd does the opposite. Two hours minimum. If you have a whole day and a car, the Udvar-Hazy annex out by Dulles has the Space Shuttle Discovery and an SR-71, and it is free too.
national-gallery-of-art: The National Gallery of Art. Free, always, and it holds the only Leonardo da Vinci painting in the Americas, a portrait called Ginevra de' Benci, in the West Building. The two buildings are joined by an underground concourse with a moving walkway under a ceiling of light, which is worth the trip by itself. Two hours in one building; do not try to do both.
arlington-national-cemetery: Arlington National Cemetery. Four hundred thousand graves, and it began as an act of spite: the land was Robert E. Lee's estate, and the Union started burying its dead in his wife's rose garden. Walk up to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier for the changing of the guard, on the hour in winter, every half hour in summer. It is guarded every minute of every day, and has been since 1937.
